entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Liu Sheng, posthumously known as Prince Jing of Zhongshan (d. 112 BCE), was a pivotal figure in the Western Han dynasty, whose life and especially his elaborate burial site provide invaluable insights into imperial power, aristocratic culture, and funerary practices of ancient China. As the son of Emperor Jing and elder brother of the formidable Emperor Wu of Han, Liu Sheng reigned over the strategically important principality of Zhongshan, located in present-day Hebei province, from 154 BCE until his death. His historical significance is primarily derived from the extraordinary archaeological discovery of his and his wife Dou Wan’s rock-cut tombs at Mancheng, which offer an unparalleled window into the elite material culture and burial rituals of the Han imperial family.

During his lifetime, Liu Sheng was known for his hedonistic lifestyle, his love of wine, and his prolific progeny, reputedly fathering over 120 sons. He famously voiced his grievances to Emperor Wu regarding the perceived restrictions on regional princes, asserting their right to enjoy life without excessive imperial oversight. Despite his flamboyant personal life, he remained a loyal prince, unlike some of his contemporaries who engaged in rebellion. His principality of Zhongshan served as a crucial buffer state in the northern regions of the empire, contributing to the stability of the Western Han during a period when central authority was still consolidating its control over semi-autonomous kingdoms.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Liu Sheng's significance stems primarily from his extraordinarily rich and well-preserved mausoleum, which has fundamentally reshaped understanding of Western Han imperial power, material culture, and funerary rituals. The artifacts from his tomb, particularly the jade burial suits, serve as critical benchmarks for Chinese archaeology.
